title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
formal:
For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous relational structure \(A\) over a finite signature, and every first-order reduct \(B\) of \(A\) with a finite relational signature, is
\[\operatorname{CSP}(B)\in\mathrm P\quad\lor\quad\operatorname{CSP}(B)\text{ is NP-complete}\ ?\]
NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The templates are fixed before the finite input is supplied. This is the unconditional complexity dichotomy, without requiring an algebraic criterion identifying the two sides.
definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a subset \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) of tuples over its domain. Countable means finite or countably infinite. Empty domains, if admitted, have trivial CSPs and do not affect the question. Nullary relations can likewise be processed separately.

The induced substructure on a subset \(S\) of a domain restricts every relation to tuples from \(S\). An embedding is an injective map \(e:D\to E\) with \(\bar d\in R^D\) if and only if \(e(\bar d)\in R^E\) for every relation and tuple; it preserves both presence and absence of relation tuples. An isomorphism is a bijective embedding, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. The structure \(A\) is homogeneous when every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of \(A\).

The structure \(A\) is finitely bounded when there is a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature such that, for every finite structure \(D\) in that signature,
\[D\text{ embeds into }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D.\]
Thus the finite patterns occurring inside \(A\) are precisely those avoiding finitely many forbidden induced patterns. Homogeneity is an additional condition, not part of finite boundedness alone.

A first-order reduct \(B\) has the same domain as \(A\). Each of its finitely many relations is defined by a fixed first-order formula over the relations of \(A\) and logical equality, using Boolean connectives and quantifiers over elements of \(A\), without naming parameters. It may forget original relations and introduce newly definable ones. Both signatures, \(A,B\), the defining formulas and a finite bound list witnessing the hypothesis are fixed; none is an input to the individual CSP.

An input \(I\) has finite domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each relation in the signature of \(B\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to B\) is any map such that \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\) implies \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^B\). It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples. The decision problem accepts exactly when such a map exists. Repeated coordinates and isolated input elements are allowed; duplicate listed tuples are harmless. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

Encode \(n\) in unary and each relation by a unary list length followed by binary tuple coordinates, in fixed signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Invalid encodings are rejected. Polynomial time means a deterministic multitape Turing machine halts correctly on every input within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for constants \(C,k\) depending on \(B\). No randomness, infinite-domain oracle, advice, supplied homomorphism, common polynomial exponent or algorithm choosing the correct side from template descriptions is required.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A problem \(Q\) is NP-hard under the stated reductions when, for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfies \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f(x)\in Q\). NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. Every CSP in the displayed scope is already known to be in NP. The two alternatives are not required to be disjoint without a separation assumption: if \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), every such problem satisfies the first alternative.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its logical negation, retaining every permitted structure and reduct. A negative answer must establish one permitted \(A,B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated many-one reductions; membership in NP already follows from the hypotheses. No separation assumption is added to the proposition. A classification for one reduct family, the first-order/logarithmic-space-hard boundary, or a procedure deciding an algebraic meta-problem does not prove the full dichotomy. The stronger algebraic tractability conjecture would suffice if proved, but is not substituted for the existing bare complexity target.
why: The main tractability-classification conjecture for well-behaved infinite-domain CSPs. It links algorithm design, universal algebra and model theory, and would extend the finite-domain dichotomy to substantially richer constraint languages.

importance.reason: A central unifying conjecture about the boundary of polynomial-time constraint solving, with broad logical scope and active links to promise CSPs.

progress.text: Bulatov and Zhuk independently prove the finite-domain CSP dichotomy; infinite domains require additional structural arguments.
Barto–Pinsker give a purely algebraic characterization of the relevant hardness obstruction for model-complete cores. The general tractability implication remains conjectural.
Bodirsky’s monograph develops the framework; the checked author postprint is dated 31 January 2026.
The revised Three Fundamental Questions paper reduces the conjecture to templates without algebraicity and strengthens links with finite-domain promise CSPs.
Dorochko–Wrona’s v3 establishes an \(FO/\mathrm{L}\)-hard dichotomy for expansions of homogeneous model-complete cores, not the full \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy.
Feller–Pinsker’s v2 provides decidability and computable-core tools under additional structural hypotheses.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026 against the January 2026 book postprint and exact primary revisions: Three Fundamental Questions v4 (6 May), FO/L-hard v3 (14 July), and Decidability of Interpretability v2 (5 August). Their introductions explicitly retain the full dichotomy as open. The July theorem has an expansion hypothesis and a lower complexity boundary; the August theorem concerns effective comparison and cores under a homogeneous Ramsey hypothesis. This is a bounded source review, not independent verification of those preprint proofs or exhaustive certification of present openness.

context_blocks.text: The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain. Homogeneity over a finite relational signature also gives quantifier elimination, so each fixed first-order reduct relation can be tested on that finite pattern by a fixed quantifier-free formula.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification. A model-complete core is a homomorphically equivalent template in which every endomorphism agrees, on each finite subset, with some automorphism; an endomorphism is a homomorphism from the template to itself.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open. Here first-order definability means that one fixed first-order sentence on finite inputs decides the CSP, and L denotes deterministic logarithmic work space.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded homogeneous Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card. The Ramsey condition says that for every pair of finite patterns P,Q and every finite number of colours, a larger finite pattern exists in which every colouring of embeddings of P has a copy of Q whose internal P-embeddings all receive one colour.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

sentences: The conjecture asks for a P-versus-NP-complete dichotomy for all finite-signature first-order reducts of countable finitely bounded homogeneous structures.
Inputs are finite constraint systems, while their possible values lie in a fixed domain that may be infinite.
Homogeneity provides symmetry, and finitely many forbidden induced patterns provide polynomial-size certificates despite the infinite domain.
Recent results simplify the conjecture’s scope or classify lower complexity boundaries, while the full tractability implication remains open in the checked sources.
A resolution would determine whether this broad structural framework rules out intermediate NP complexity.
